titles: The House Where Goya Painted His Nightmares
Nobody Was Supposed to See These Paintings
youtube.description_lead: In 1819, a deaf, 72-year-old Francisco de Goya bought a farmhouse outside Madrid and covered two of its rooms with fourteen nightmares. He never titled them, never signed them and never wrote a word about them. This is the story of the Black Paintings: why he painted them, how they were peeled off the walls, and why some historians once doubted he painted them at all.

facts.claim: Goya bought the Quinta del Sordo on 27 February 1819, from a previous owner who was deaf; he was 72
An illness at 46 (1792-93) left Goya deaf
Leocadia Weiss (1790-1856) lived with him at the Quinta with her daughter Rosario (b. 1814)
He wanted distance from the court of Ferdinand VII

Late 1819 acute illness; Self-Portrait with Dr Arrieta (1820, Minneapolis Institute of Art) and its inscription (card: 'Goya thankful, to his friend Arrieta… at the end of 1819, at seventy-three years of age.')
14 murals in oil directly on the plaster of two rooms, c. 1820-23, painted over earlier rural scenes; never titled, signed or written about
Saturn traditionally faced La Leocadia; the eyes were badly damaged and repainted
Rubens's Saturn (1636-38) for the king; calm vs Goya's madness; Ciofalo: the victim appears to be an adult; claim of an erased sexual detail
1823 restoration of absolutism; house signed over to grandson Mariano in 1823; hiding at priest José Duaso's; 2 May 1824 request to take the waters at Plombières
Goya died in Bordeaux on 16 April 1828, aged 82; he did not write of the Black Paintings
Mariano gave the house to Javier in 1830 and inherited it again in 1854; bought by Émile d'Erlanger in 1873
J. Laurent photographed the murals in situ in 1874; transfer to canvas by Salvador Martínez Cubells, the Prado's chief restorer, with extensive repainting
Witches' Sabbath was cut, possibly to fit a space in Paris; shown at the Trocadéro, 20 May - 10 Nov 1878; donated to the State (decree 20 Dec 1881)
Hamerton (The Portfolio, 1879) called Goya a 'monster of immorality, impudence, and ingratitude'
Junquera (2003): one-storey records, Javier as author, Mariano selling; Glendinning 'totally unconvinced'; the Prado accepts them
Antonio Saura called The Dog 'the world's most beautiful picture'
